reason: Children give the scriptural proof and a substantive reasoned argument for accepting the term cognitive obscuration.
Subject and purpose are one-line definitions, but the ultimate-purpose and connection children explain the verse and discuss who first taught the Abhidharma.
Each unconditioned dharma is explained with definition, nature, divisions raised as a question, etymology and an example.
Number and order of the eight chapters are argued at length, with only the third child a pointer.
Children explain the basis and synonyms of conditioned and contaminated dharmas with etymologies and reasons.
Each child simply lists the divisions of one sense object (form, sound, taste, smell, touch) with no discussion.
Divisions, function and characteristics of the elements are glossed, and the fourth child raises and resolves a doubt about earth versus earth-element.
Children give the nature and divisions of feeling, perception, formations and the dharma-sphere as plain definitions.
Children identify the mind-element with textual analysis and argue against an objection about the count of eighteen elements.
Children explain how the aggregates, sources and elements include all dharmas and argue whether inclusion is real or nominal.
Children answer why three sets were taught, why feeling and perception are separate aggregates, and why the unconditioned is not an aggregate, with objections and citations.
Children argue the order of the aggregates and faculties at length and resolve a doubt about naming the form and dharma sources.
Children set out rival views on the size of a dharma-aggregate and then the author's own position with its scriptural basis.
Children answer a doubt about the space and consciousness elements, noting the Sautrantika dissent and the reasoning.
Each child is a one-line definition of one of the three kinds of obstruction.
Children classify the elements by ethical quality and realm, raising and answering objections about the form realm.
Children classify the elements by contamination, conceptuality and object with extended reasoning and a sutra-contradiction resolved.
Children classify material elements in five ways, each with reasons, and report divergent views of earlier masters.
Children classify the elements by three origins, answering a scriptural objection and explaining the exceptions.
Children discuss active and inactive faculties with tenet analysis and the divergent Kashmiri and Western views.
Children classify what is abandoned by seeing or meditation and refute the Vatsiputriya view with formal reasoning.
Children investigate who sees, notably debating whether the eye or eye-consciousness sees across Vaibhashika and Sautrantika views.
Children answer whether faculties contact and match their objects, each with reasons and examples.
Children answer why the faculty rather than the object is called the support and names the consciousness, with reasons and analogies.
Children only state the general rule and its one exception about the level of nose, tongue and body.
Children present the Vaibhashika and Sautrantika explanations of the faculties' dominance at length with citations.
Children define the pain and pleasure faculties, adding only a brief gloss on third-dhyana mental pleasure.
Children define mental pleasure and displeasure with a one-line distinction, no discussion of their own.
Children give a one-line definition of equanimity and a one-sentence reason it is not split into bodily and mental.
Children classify the faculties six ways with reasons, the second including an extended discussion of the life faculty with citations.
The general-rule child raises and answers an objection about the mind faculty, while the exception child enumerates cases for apparitional birth.
Each child is a one-line count of which faculties cease at death for apparitional and womb birth.
Children explain which faculties attain each fruit under different conditions and resolve a contradiction with another treatise.
